questions.prompt: A client asks a technique question you do not know. You are tempted to invent a confident medical claim. What should you do?
options: Say “I don't know,” then add “Let me find out.” “I don't know” is honesty, not stupidity. Not knowing is temporary; refusing to learn can become permanent.
Guess confidently so you do not appear uninformed.
Pretend you know because leadership requires an instant answer.
Change the subject and hope they forget.

questions.prompt: You are LT. A less experienced therapist corrects your pressure. Ego wants you to dismiss them. What is the trap?
options: When you become more committed to appearing knowledgeable than becoming knowledgeable, you sacrifice growth for appearance. Real growth begins when you can say “Teach me.”
Correction from juniors is always wrong.
You must immediately change company protocol.

questions.prompt: You are not a leader. After a 4-hands session you refuse Therapist Review because “I already know my style.” What failed?
options: Teachability as a life skill, not only a leadership topic. Search, process, act, reflect — learning is a way of living.

questions.prompt: You only read comments that praise your routine and reject any challenge. What are you searching for?
options: Confirmation. We say we want knowledge, but sometimes what we actually want is confirmation.

questions.prompt: You learn a safer draping method, then never apply it on the floor. Which step did you skip?
options: ACT: “Let me apply what I've learned.” Knowledge without action is incomplete.

questions.prompt: A client gives feedback that pressure was uneven. You immediately defend instead of thinking. What should come first after the gap is visible?
options: THINK: “Let me examine this.” Then SEARCH and PROCESS — being teachable is not believing everything, but reflecting: Could I be wrong?

questions.prompt: You tell a colleague, “I don't know, and I'm not interested in knowing.” How does the article name this?
options: A mindset problem. There is a powerful difference between “I don't know” and “I don't know, and I'm not interested in knowing.”

questions.prompt: In communication with a tense client, you refuse to listen because you already planned your speech. Which teachable line is missing?
options: “I may not know. Let me listen.”

questions.prompt: After trying a new sequence, you never ask what worked. What did you skip in the framework?
options: REFLECT: What happened? What worked? What didn't? What should I change?

questions.prompt: A SM asks you to investigate a recurring client complaint. You answer instantly without checking. What maturity sign is missing?
options: Never too proud to ask a question, never too defensive to reconsider, never too comfortable to keep learning.
Protecting ego in front of staff.

title: SECTION B — FILL IN THE GAP

questions.prompt: Complete: “Not knowing is temporary. Refusing to learn can become _____."
Complete the framework: “ADMIT → THINK → SEARCH → PROCESS → ACT → _____."
Complete: “The problem isn't that we don't know everything. The problem begins when we are unwilling to _____ what we don't know.”
Complete: “Without reflection, you can accumulate information without actually developing _____."
Complete: “When you become more committed to appearing knowledgeable than becoming knowledgeable, you will eventually sacrifice growth for _____."
The deeper topic of the article is…
options: teachability as a life skill. Leadership is just one application. It is framed around how we respond when we discover that we don't know.
how to never say I don't know.

questions.prompt: In section 1, after saying “I don't know,” what should you add?
PROCESS in the framework means…
options: Let me understand and evaluate what I've found.

questions.prompt: The article says you don't become less because somebody knows something you don't. Someone knowing more in one area…
options: makes them more valuable as a person.
does not make them more valuable than you. It simply means they know something you haven't learned yet.

questions.prompt: The closing says learning is not an event. It is…
